title: Episode 143: Ulysses S. Grant and the Gentleman's Peace: Appomattox and the Terms of Reconciliation
description:
On Palm Sunday, April 9, 1865, inside the parlor of a brick farmhouse in the village of Appomattox Court House, Virginia, the bloodiest war in American history reached its quiet, astonishing conclusion. Ulysses S. Grant—the relentless butcher of the Wilderness, wearing a mud-spattered private's blouse—sat down across a marble table from General Robert E. Lee, dressed in immaculate dress gray with an engraved ceremonial sword. What followed was not a vengeful triumph of conqueror over vanquished, but an act of unprecedented magnanimity that astonished the world. Discover the forgotten details of the negotiations, the order to let the Confederate soldiers keep their horses for the spring plowing, and Grant's immediate command to silence the Union victory cannon: 'The rebels are our countrymen again.'

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we enter the parlor of Wilmer McLean in the sleepy crossroads of Appomattox Court House, Virginia, on Palm Sunday of 1865. The meeting between Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee would decide the fate of twenty-five thousand starving Confederate soldiers and set the moral tone for the reunification of the United States. In an age of total war, Grant chose radical grace. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE MAN FROM POINT PLEASANT
If a novelist had invented the life of Ulysses S. Grant prior to 1861, readers would have rejected it as utterly implausible. Born in a tiny two-room cottage in Point Pleasant, Ohio, in 1822, Hiram Ulysses Grant was a shy, unassuming boy with an extraordinary, almost mystical gift for horsemanship. When his father enrolled him at West Point without his knowledge, an administrative clerical error enrolled him as 'Ulysses S. Grant'—a mistake Grant gladly accepted to avoid the unfortunate initials H.U.G. Though he served with quiet gallantry as a quartermaster during the Mexican-American War, the peacetime army bored him to despair. Stationed at remote outposts in California and Oregon, separated from his beloved wife Julia and young children, Grant turned to alcohol to numb his loneliness and resigned his commission in disgrace in 1854.

The seven years that followed were an agonizing parade of humiliations. Grant tried farming on an eighty-acre plot of land near St. Louis given to him by his father-in-law, building a rough log cabin with his own hands that he wryly named 'Hardscrabble.' Crop failure and malaria forced him to pawn his gold watch for twenty-two dollars just to buy Christmas presents for his children. He tried selling firewood on street corners, working in a real estate office, and finally swallowed his pride to work as an unpaid clerk in his father's leather and harness store in Galena, Illinois, under the supervision of his younger brothers. By age thirty-nine, neighbors viewed him as a broken, harmless failure. Yet when Confederate cannon opened fire on Fort Sumter in April 1861, this quiet clerk possessed the two qualities modern warfare demanded above all else: an absolute lack of physical fear and a relentless, mathematical understanding that war was about the destruction of armies, not the occupation of terrain.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE OVERLAND GRIND AND THE SIEGE OF PETERSBURG
Four years of devastating carnage transformed the Galena leather clerk into Lieutenant General of all United States Armies—a rank previously held only by George Washington. After brilliant triumphs at Fort Donelson, Shiloh, Vicksburg, and Chattanooga, Lincoln summoned Grant to the East in March 1864 to take command of the entire Union war effort. While previous Union commanders in Virginia had retreated after every bloody setback against Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia, Grant refused to step backward. Following the horrific bloodbath in the Wilderness in May 1864, Grant rode to the head of his columns and turned his horse to the right—marching southward toward Richmond. Veterans of the Army of the Potomac wept with joy; at last, they had a general who would not turn back.

What followed was the grueling ten-month siege of Petersburg. Entrenched in miles of muddy trenches and earthworks, Grant relentlessly stretched Lee's shrinking lines to the breaking point. By March 1865, Lee's army was starving, barefoot, and riddled with desertion. On April 2, Grant broke through the Confederate lines at Petersburg, forcing Lee to evacuate Richmond. The Confederate capital was set ablaze by retreating rebel troops. For seven agonizing days, Grant's cavalry under Philip Sheridan raced ahead of Lee's retreating army, cutting off their supply trains and hemming them in along the Appomattox River. On the night of April 8, Sheridan captured Lee's ration trains at Appomattox Station and threw his cavalry across the western road. Lee was surrounded on three sides. His cavalry commander, John B. Gordon, sent word to Lee: 'My corps has been fought to a frazzle, and I fear I can do nothing more without heavy reinforcements.' Lee looked down at the ground and whispered softly: 'Then there is nothing left for me to do but to go and see General Grant, and I would rather die a thousand deaths.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE PARLOR OF WILMER MCLEAN
By one of the most astonishing ironies in military history, the American Civil War began and ended on the property of the same man. In July 1861, Wilmer McLean was a wholesale grocer living near Manassas, Virginia. A Confederate cannonball smashed through the roof of his kitchen during the First Battle of Bull Run as General P.G.T. Beauregard was eating dinner. Desperate to escape the horrors of war and protect his family, McLean packed up his household and moved two hundred miles southwest to the tiny, sleepy village of Appomattox Court House. Four years later, on Palm Sunday, April 9, 1865, a Confederate courier rode into the village seeking a suitable home for two commanding generals to meet. McLean reluctantly agreed, opening his elegant two-story red brick home with a wide wooden front porch. The war had found him again.

Robert E. Lee arrived first, around one o'clock in the afternoon, accompanied only by his military secretary, Colonel Charles Marshall. Lee cut an imposing, majestic figure. Standing over six feet tall with silver hair and an aristocratic beard, he wore an immaculate, brand-new Confederate general's uniform of deep cadet gray, complete with gold-embroidered cuffs, a red silk sash, polished black dress boots with golden spurs, and an exquisite engraved dress sword presented to him by admirers in England. Thirty minutes later, the clatter of iron horseshoes echoed on the gravel road. Ulysses S. Grant dismounted on the lawn and walked briskly onto the porch.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: MUD-SPATTERED BLUE AND IMMACULATE GRAY
The contrast between the two men who met in Wilmer McLean's front parlor could not have been more striking. While Lee looked like the living embodiment of a noble, classical knight from an ancient age of chivalry, Grant looked like a weary, mud-caked foot soldier. Having ridden hard for hours through dust and swamp from his headquarters, Grant wore a simple private's dark blue flannel blouse, with only the three silver stars of a lieutenant general pinned to his rumpled shoulder straps to denote his rank. His trousers were tucked into muddy, unpolished leather boots, and he carried neither sword nor sidearm. He was forty-two years old, slouched, and covered in road dust.

Grant later admitted in his personal memoirs that despite the enormous victory, his feelings that afternoon were anything but triumphant: 'I felt like anything rather than rejoicing at the downfall of a foe who had fought so long and valiantly, and had suffered so much for a cause, though that cause was, I believe, one of the worst for which a people ever fought.' To break the crushing awkwardness of the moment, Grant began reminiscing about their service together in the Mexican War nearly two decades earlier. Lee politely recalled meeting Grant in Mexico, but after several minutes of polite military small talk, Lee gently steered the conversation back to the painful reality at hand: 'I suppose, General Grant, that the object of our present meeting is to ascertain the terms upon which you would receive the surrender of my army.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: WRITTEN IN A FIELD DESK: THE GENIUS OF MAGNANIMITY
Grant called for his portable wooden field desk and sat down at a small oval table. Dipping his steel pen into black ink, he drafted the surrender terms on the spot in his clear, rapid hand. What Grant wrote in that quiet Virginia parlor altered the course of American history. He did not demand that Lee's soldiers be marched into prisoner-of-war camps; he did not demand the arrest of officers for treason; he did not demand that Lee hand over his sword in humiliation. Instead, Grant proposed that the entire Army of Northern Virginia surrender their rifles, artillery, and battle flags, sign individual paroles promising not to take up arms against the United States again, and then return peacefully to their homes.

Most importantly, Grant inserted a crucial legal shield at the end of the terms: 'This done, each officer and man will be allowed to return to their homes, not to be disturbed by United States authority so long as they observe their paroles and the laws in force where they may reside.' By guaranteeing that paroled Confederate soldiers could not be disturbed by federal authorities, Grant unilaterally immunized every soldier in Lee's army from federal prosecution for treason—a protection he would personally and fiercely defend against President Andrew Johnson just weeks later. When Lee read the handwritten draft, his stern expression softened visibly. He looked up at Grant and remarked with genuine emotion: 'This will have the best possible effect upon the men. It will be very gratifying, and will do much toward conciliating our people.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: LET THE MEN KEEP THEIR HORSES FOR THE SPRING PLOWING
As the two generals reviewed the terms, Lee pointed out a practical dilemma. In the Confederate army, unlike the United States regular army, the cavalrymen and artillery drivers owned their own personal horses and mules. Under the strict wording of Grant's terms, these animals would be surrendered as military property. Lee noted that the men's homes were ruined, the planting season was upon them, and without horses, the South would starve. Without a moment's hesitation, Grant declined to alter the formal written document, but gave Lee his personal word as Commander-in-Chief:

'I will not change the terms as written,' Grant said calmly, 'but I will instruct my officers to let every man of the Confederate army who claims to own a horse or mule take the animal home with him. They will need them to put in a crop to carry themselves and their families through the coming winter.' Lee was deeply touched. 'This will have the happiest result,' he said. Lee then admitted that his men had been living on parched corn for days and were completely starving. Grant instantly dispatched an order to his quartermasters: twenty-five thousand Union rations of beef, hardtack, sugar, and coffee were immediately distributed to the famished Confederate lines. The conqueror was feeding the vanquished before the ink on the surrender papers was even dry.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: SILENCING THE VICTORY GUNS
Around four o'clock in the afternoon, the meeting concluded. Robert E. Lee stepped onto the McLean porch, signaled for his gray horse Traveller, and mounted up. As Lee rode slowly down the lane, Ulysses S. Grant stepped onto the porch. Removing his slouched campaign hat, Grant bowed in silent, respectful tribute. Lee returned the salute, lifted his hat, and rode back to break the heartbreaking news to his weeping veterans. Moments later, word of the surrender spread through the Union encampments. Nearby Union artillery batteries suddenly unlimbered their guns and began firing thunderous, celebratory 100-gun victory salutes that shook the valley.

Grant heard the cannon fire and immediately dispatched a staff officer at a dead gallop with a stern order: 'Stop that firing! The war is over. The rebels are our countrymen again, and the best sign of rejoicing after the victory will be to abstain from all demonstrations in the field.' Three days later, on April 12, when Confederate General John B. Gordon led the remnants of Lee's infantry to formally stack their muskets, Union Major General Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain—the hero of Little Round Top—ordered his Union troops to snap to attention and execute the 'carry arms' salute, the highest military honor one soldier can pay another. In the ashes of America's deadliest war, the spirit of Appomattox demonstrated that true strength lay not in vengeance, but in the courage of reconciliation.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Ulysses S. Grant's magnanimity at Appomattox stands as one of the finest moments in American military annals. By choosing grace over retribution, he helped prevent a protracted guerrilla insurgency and laid the foundation for a reunited nation. Next week, we examine Grant's second great historic challenge: his presidency, and his fearless, relentless campaign to dismantle the Ku Klux Klan and defend the civil rights of newly freed citizens across the South. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
